extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, mathematical graduate students, and the mathematical community evaluating or producing mathematical research
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what constitutes 'good mathematics' across many dimensions (problem solving, technique, theory, exposition, etc.), intended to inform how mathematical research is produced and judged within fields and by the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: A major breakthrough on an important mathematical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: solving a central open problem; valued as a distinct type of mathematical achievement. Tactical relevance: fields in need of problem solutions may prioritise this quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A masterful use of existing methods or the development of new tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes creation or skilful application of methods that advance the toolbox of the field; such techniques may later enable many other results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceptual framework or choice of notation which systematically unifies and generalises an existing body of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory-building organises previously disjoint results and suggests new directions; valued especially in mature fields that need organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical insight
rubrics_metrics.description: A major conceptual simplification or the realisation of a unifying principle, heuristic, analogy, or theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often yields clearer understanding and can guide future work; examples include discovering the right viewpoint that simplifies problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The revelation of an unexpected and intriguing new mathematical phenomenon, connection, or counterexample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery can open new directions or expose limits of current approaches (e.g., Behrend's counterexample shaping feasible methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications to important problems in physics, engineering, computer science, statistics, or from one field of mathematics to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates usefulness beyond pure theory; cross-disciplinary impact increases perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A detailed and informative survey on a timely topic or a clear and well-motivated argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposition and surveys help disseminate ideas, attract interest, and train others; valued as a distinct contribution (e.g., Furstenberg's book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: A lecture or writing style which enables others to learn and do mathematics more effectively, or contributions to mathematical education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical clarity can increase the impact and longevity of ideas by making them accessible to newcomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical vision
rubrics_metrics.description: A long-range and fruitful program or set of conjectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vision guides research direction, proposes grand problems and frameworks (e.g., influential conjectures or programs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A research goal which is inherently interesting and impacts important topics, themes, or questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting problems or approaches with intrinsic interest and broader relevance; taste affects field development and attractiveness to newcomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematical public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective showcasing of a mathematical achievement to non-mathematicians or from one field of mathematics to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication and publicity can attract attention, talent, and resources; helps a field remain vibrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good meta-mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Advances in the foundations, philosophy, history, scholarship, or practice of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on foundations or history can reshape understanding of what mathematics is and how it should be practiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: All details correctly and carefully given in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigour is essential but is only one component of quality; some advances may be heuristically important even before fully rigorous implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Results that are amazing/striking (e.g., Ramanujan identities) or easy-to-state but hard-to-prove theorems that have aesthetic appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beauty is subjective but historically influential; beautiful statements often attract deep study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegant mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Achieving a difficult result with a minimum of effort or complexity (e.g., 'proofs from The Book').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegance (concise, simple proofs) is prized, but should not replace originality or deeper discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A radically new and original technique, viewpoint, or species of result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Radical originality can transform fields; creative approaches may initially be risky but highly rewarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Useful mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A lemma or method which will be used repeatedly in future work on the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usefulness (reusability) is a strong indicator of lasting impact; methods like the Szemerédi regularity lemma exemplify this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A sharp result that matches known counterexamples or that deduces an unexpectedly strong conclusion from a seemingly weak hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharpness and optimality heighten value; quantitative bounds and matching lower bounds matter (e.g., Gowers' quantitative bounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deep mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A result which is manifestly non-trivial, capturing a subtle phenomenon beyond elementary tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth often corresponds to conceptual difficulty and reveals novel structure; such results may require new theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuitive mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument which is natural and easily visualisable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition aids understanding and communication; intuitive proofs or heuristics can guide rigorous development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitive mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A classification of all objects of a certain type, or the 'final word' on a mathematical topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness/classification results close a subject area and serve as reference points for future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part of a greater mathematical story
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical work that fits into a larger narrative, leading to many further pieces of good mathematics across different dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao emphasises that the very best mathematics not only satisfies local criteria but also integrates into and generates long-term developments and interactions with other results and fields; this global fit can be more predictive of lasting value than local measures alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-dependent priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of which qualities of mathematical progress to prize depends on the state of each field (mature vs. nascent) and tactical considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mature fields, theory/unification and rigor may be emphasised; in newer fields, conjecture-making, experimentation, and non-rigorous heuristics may be more productive. Communities should maintain an evolving consensus on priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and diversity of qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pursuing only one or two qualities (e.g., only elegance or only generalisation) to the neglect of others, as this can harm a field's long-term health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao lists anti-patterns (ornate technical generalisation without direction; many conjectures with no progress; ad hoc problem collection with no unifying theme; overly dry formal recasting; reverence for classical results without new originality) to illustrate harms of imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolving consensus and tactical adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for what counts as good mathematics should be periodically updated and debated within fields and by outsiders, responsive to the field's needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communities should detect and correct imbalances and shift emphasis as the field develops; resource allocation (prizes, journals) can reflect multiple valued qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some qualities require hindsight and are subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: Many desirable qualities are difficult to measure immediately and are somewhat subjective, making rigorous definitions problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao warns against arrogance in attempting absolute definitions; rigour is an exception but other qualities often need historical perspective to judge fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good mathematics begets more good mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A phenomenon where work strong in one sense tends to generate further work strong in other senses, suggesting a quasi-universal notion of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao conjectures that high-quality mathematics often leads to additional advances (techniques, applications, exposition), as illustrated by the Szemerédi theorem story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial or heuristic results can be valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical work need not be absolutely correct in every detail to be useful to future rigorous work; heuristic, inchoate, or partially-correct ideas can stimulate progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao notes examples where incorrect constructions were later repaired but still provided crucial structure (e.g., constructions around prime gaps), arguing for tolerance of preliminary, influential work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative bounds and trade-offs matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of quantitative estimates (e.g., bounds) and awareness of inherent limitations (e.g., tower-type lower bounds) are important criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: van der Waerden's original bounds were astronomically large; Gowers and others improved quantitative bounds. Understanding quantitative limitations guides method selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-methodological convergence and transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing different proofs/approaches (combinatorial, ergodic, Fourier, hypergraph) that interrelate or can be transferred across contexts is a sign of richness and robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tao highlights multiple independent proofs of Szemerédi’s theorem and subsequent transference principles (e.g., relative Szemerédi) as evidence of depth and usefulness; convergence often spurs further advances.
